name: typed-collection
intent: Give each group of domain objects its own type, so the rules that govern the group - which elements may join, how many, in what combination - are owned and enforced by that type instead of being re-checked by every caller that receives a bare collection.
problem: A multi-valued domain attribute (an aggregate's line items, a roster, a price list) travels as a generic container: any caller can add, remove, clear or replace elements, so the group's rules end up in comments or in duplicated guard code and derived state drifts out of step. Only the container's representation is fixed in every signature; the group's behaviour and vocabulary are not - totals, ordering and selection are recomputed at each call site. Where the language has generics the element type is at least checked, but the invariants of the group itself remain unowned.
context: Model code that owns multi-valued attributes: aggregate roots and entities with child collections, value objects that are collections (a price list, a roster, a route), repositories that hand hydrated collections to the model, and the application services that keep the model's vocabulary at their boundary. It pays off when the group has rules or derived behaviour of its own; it does not apply to collections that are only transport (DTOs, message payloads) or to a local variable inside one method.
benefits: Membership and aggregation invariants get one enforcement point: every construction and every mutation passes through the collection's own code, so an invalid group cannot exist instead of being discovered later.
Callers can no longer mutate behind the owner's back, so derived state (counts, totals, registered events) stays consistent without defensive re-checks.
The domain vocabulary returns: orders.add(lineItem), roster.contains(member), priceList.total() read as the model instead of generic list operations scattered across services.
Collection-level behaviour - ordering, selection, aggregation, joining - lives next to the elements it operates on instead of being duplicated in each consumer.
The representation becomes replaceable: a list, a set, a sorted structure or a lazily loaded, persisted form can be swapped without touching callers, because only the collection's API is public.
Signatures carry meaning: Orders, Roster or PriceList tells a reader what the group is and what may be done with it, whereas List<Order> has to be decoded from the surrounding code.
tradeoffs: One extra type per collection concept, and the boilerplate is real: with no collection plumbing to inherit - the original objection to typed collections - the type must implement iteration and the language's standard interfaces itself.

Callers lose generic-collection conveniences (bulk operations, LINQ/streams, library functions typed on List/Seq/Array) unless the type implements the standard interfaces or converts, i.e. copies, at the boundary.

Exposure costs something either way: a defensive copy allocates per access, an unmodifiable view or frozen array is cheaper but reflects later mutations or throws at surprising moments, and every caller must be told which semantics it got.
Framework friction: ORMs, serializers and mapping layers expect their own collection conventions, so a custom collection type usually needs a mapping hook or a conversion at the edge.
Wrapping a group that has no rules is pure indirection - the type, the conversion and the extra layer buy nothing unless the collection actually owns invariants or behaviour.
Mutation policy must be uniform: mixing in-place add/remove with methods that return new instances produces aliasing surprises that are harder to debug than the leak the pattern removed.

participants.responsibility: The domain type itself (Orders, Roster, PriceList): owns the elements, exposes intention-revealing operations and refuses or repairs illegal membership.
The domain object the collection admits - usually an Entity or Value Object; its identity rules decide what counts as a duplicate.
The aggregate or entity (sometimes a service) that holds the collection and delegates the multi-valued rules to it instead of enforcing them itself.
Reads elements through iteration, an unmodifiable view or a snapshot, and changes the group only through the collection's named methods.
The exposure mechanism - unmodifiable view, defensive copy, slice/span, iterator - that lets a client traverse the elements without reaching the container.

use_cases: An aggregate root whose line items must stay within configured limits and whose total is derived: Orders enforces both in one place instead of in every service that adds a line.
A roster or participant list with a uniqueness rule (no duplicate member id or email) that must hold for every mutation, not only for the batch that first created it.
A price list whose elements must all share one currency and whose sum has domain meaning - the MoneyList case, where sum() can never run on an empty or mixed list.
A bounded queue of pending work (at most N open jobs) that must reject additions instead of growing without limit.
A repository read path that returns Orders or PriceList instead of List<Peer>, keeping the domain language alive in the application layer.
A collection that carries real queries - next available slot, oldest unpaid invoice, orders by date - so each query has a home instead of being spelled out repeatedly.

TYPO3 Extbase models every multi-valued relation on a domain object as a typed ObjectStorage property - initialized in initializeObject(), mutated only through the model's addX()/removeX() methods, and unique by object identity - exactly the first-class-collection form the pattern prescribes (https://docs.typo3.org/m/typo3/reference-coreapi/main/en-us/ExtensionArchitecture/Extbase/Persistence/Relations.html).

Doctrine ORM hands each entity's multi-valued association to a Collection - an ArrayCollection or lazily hydrating PersistentCollection - that owns iteration, filtering and removal semantics (removing an element unlinks the association, never the entity), so the framework itself, and the custom collectionClass hook for rules of one's own, use the domain group as a type rather than a raw array (https://www.doctrine-project.org/projects/doctrine-orm/en/current/reference/working-with-associations.html).
avoid_when: The group is a transport bag: a DTO, message payload or serialization boundary where the shape must stay generic and no rule is attached.
The only requirement is immutability: return an immutable or read-only type (ReadonlyArray, tuple, List.copyOf, unmodifiable view) instead of inventing a domain type with no behaviour.
Generics plus one validation at the edge already express the rule, and nothing about the group has behaviour of its own - Fowler's 'not worth the trouble' case for typed collections.
The framework at that boundary insists on a standard container and conversion code would dominate the change.
It is a private local collection inside one method: there is no API surface to protect and the extra type is ceremony.
anti_patterns: Leaky wrapper: a collection class whose getter, Items property or public field still returns the internal list, so every invariant can be bypassed.
Rule-free typed list: EmployeeList/ModelList that only narrows the element type and enforces nothing - boilerplate with the original objection intact.
God collection: every query, sort, projection and report that any service happens to need, turning the type into an unrelated grab bag.
Mixed mutation semantics: in-place add/remove next to methods returning new collections, so callers cannot predict whether their reference changed.
Defensive-copy-everywhere: a fresh list allocated on every read in a hot path, in the name of safety.
design_principles: Encapsulation: the object that owns the data controls every change to it - tell the collection what to do instead of asking for the list and mutating it.
Single responsibility: the group's rules and behaviour have exactly one home.
Information hiding: the container and its representation stay internal; only domain operations and traversal are public.
Make illegal states unrepresentable: validation in constructors and mutators means an invalid group cannot be built.
Composition over inheritance: wrap the framework container rather than inheriting from it, so its convenience API does not become your API.
best_practices: Expose reads as an unmodifiable view, a copy or a slice/span, and keep mutations behind intention-revealing methods; never return the internal container or an upcast of it.
Validate in the constructor and in every mutator, including bulk paths, and decide deliberately between fail-fast exceptions and Result/Either returns.
Name the type after the domain concept (Orders, Roster, PriceList), not after the element type plus List.
Implement the language's standard iteration or collection interface so for-in, map/filter and library functions keep working; convert explicitly at framework boundaries.
Make identity rules explicit - what makes two elements duplicates - and enforce them where elements enter the collection, not in a later cleanup pass.
Keep whole-collection replacement explicit (replaceAll/clear) instead of exposing a setter for the container.
sources: Martin Fowler, 'Typed Collection', martinfowler.com bliki (17 June 2003) - names the per-domain-type collection and argues that the boilerplate is only worth it when the collection carries rules of its own.
Martin Fowler, 'Encapsulated Collection', martinfowler.com bliki - do not return the collection data structure itself; provide add/remove methods plus a read-only view or a copy.

Jeff Bay, 'Object Calisthenics', rule 4 'First-class collections' (The ThoughtWorks Anthology, 2008) - each collection gets wrapped in its own class so that behaviour related to it has a home; rule quoted at https://softwareengineering.stackexchange.com/questions/139353/why-should-we-preferably-use-first-class-collections

Doctrine ORM, 'Working with associations' (official documentation) - multi-valued associations hydrate into a first-class Collection (ArrayCollection/PersistentCollection) that owns lazy loading, a filtering API and unlink-only removal semantics; https://www.doctrine-project.org/projects/doctrine-orm/en/current/reference/working-with-associations.html

TYPO3 CMS Core Reference, 'Object relations in Extbase' (official documentation) - multi-valued relations on Extbase domain models are typed ObjectStorage properties managed through addX()/removeX(); https://docs.typo3.org/m/typo3/reference-coreapi/main/en-us/ExtensionArchitecture/Extbase/Persistence/Relations.html

Vladimir Khorikov, 'Collections and Primitive Obsession' (Enterprise Craftsmanship) - counterweight criticism: many collections need no class of their own because the owning entity can hold the invariant and expose a controlled API; a separate collection type pays off only for root-level groups with behaviour of their own; https://enterprisecraftsmanship.com/posts/collections-primitive-obsession/
